Tous s'accordent sur le point final : « Vers ton Seigneur, ce jour-là, sera la conduite », c'est-à-dire le retour de chacun vers le jugement divin, vers le Paradis ou vers le Feu.

Ce verset décrit le moment de l'agonie, lorsque l'âme atteint la clavicule et la gorge, et que le mourant prend conscience que c'est la séparation d'avec le monde. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général : il s'agit de l'extrême angoisse de la mort. Ils divergent sur plusieurs expressions. Pour « Qui peut guérir ? » (man raqin), Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu Qilaba et al-Dahhak y voient une demande de médecin ou de guérisseur pour le malade, tandis qu'Ibn 'Abbas, Sulayman al-Taymi, Muqatil et Abu al-Jawza' attribuent la question aux anges qui se demandent qui emportera l'âme, des anges de la miséricorde ou ceux du châtiment. Quant à « les deux jambes s'enlacent », Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan et al-Rabi' l'interprètent comme l'union de la détresse de ce monde et de celle de l'au-delà, al-Sha'bi, Abu Malik et Qatada comme le mouvement des jambes du mourant, et al-Hasan et Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab comme les jambes enveloppées dans le linceul. Al-Tabari retient, en s'appuyant sur l'usage arabe de « la guerre s'est dressée sur sa jambe », que c'est l'union de la douleur de la mort et de l'effroi de l'instant qui suit. Le terme « al-masaq » désigne le retour vers Dieu, compris par certains comme le lieu où l'on va, par d'autres comme la demeure finale. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et d'autres rapportent ces avis sans trancher nettement.

Ce verset décrit l'agonie : lorsque l'âme atteint les clavicules, c'est-à-dire la gorge et le haut de la poitrine, la détresse s'accroît, et l'on demande autour du mourant s'il existe un guérisseur capable de le soigner. Le mourant comprend alors qu'il quitte ce monde, ses proches et ses biens. L'expression « et la jambe se mêle à la jambe » désigne, selon Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Rabi' ibn Anas et Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, la jonction de la fin de la vie d'ici-bas avec le début de la vie dernière, et l'accumulation des épreuves ; al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir retiennent cette lecture. Qatada, Mujahid et al-Dahhak y voient l'intensité de l'angoisse de la mort et de l'effroi du passage : les hommes préparent le corps tandis que les anges préparent l'âme. D'autres comprennent qu'il s'agit des deux jambes du défunt : Ash-Sha'bi, Qatada et Abu Malik y voient leur enroulement à l'agonie, al-Hasan et Ibn al-Musayyib leur enveloppement dans le linceul, et al-Hasan rapporte aussi qu'elles cessent de le porter. Quant à la parole « qui le soignera ? », certains commentateurs la prêtent aux proches du malade, tandis qu'Ibn Abbas et Abu al-Jawza la rapportent aux anges qui se demandent qui élèvera l'âme. Le verset se termine par « vers ton Seigneur, ce jour-là, sera la conduite », c'est-à-dire le retour au jugement de Dieu, vers le paradis ou vers le feu, que les commentateurs présentent comme une affirmation de la résurrection et de la rétribution.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset décrit le moment de l'agonie : lorsque l'âme parvient à la clavicule, c'est-à-dire à la base de la gorge, les proches demandent s'il existe quelqu'un pour la guérir par une incantation ou un traitement, et le mourant comprend qu'il quitte la vie, ses proches et ses biens. Presque tous s'accordent à dire que « le mensuel » désigne le fait d'être conduit vers Dieu et vers Son jugement, où l'on est mené soit au Paradis, soit au Feu. Pour la question de savoir qui prononce « qui pourrait le guérir ? », Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilaba, Qatada, 'Ikrima et Ibn Zayd l'entendent comme une demande de soin, tandis qu'Abu al-Jawza' et Abu al-'Aliya comprennent qu'il s'agit des anges demandant qui emportera l'âme vers le ciel, qu'ils soient anges de miséricorde ou anges du châtiment. L'expression « la jambe s'enlace à la jambe » a reçu plusieurs interprétations : Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi' et Qatada y voient une image de la rencontre de l'épreuve de la vie d'ici-bas avec celle de l'au-delà, ou de la grande détresse, et al-Tabari retient cette lecture comme la plus juste. Al-Hasan et Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab y voient la réalité physique des jambes enveloppées dans le linceul, tandis que al-Dahhak évoque les vivants qui préparent le corps pendant que les anges préparent l'âme. Quant à « il crut que c'était la séparation », la plupart comprennent qu'il en eut la certitude, puisque l'événement n'était pas encore survenu.

Ce passage décrit le mécréant obstiné, que la plupart des commentateurs identifient à Abu Jahl : il n'a ni cru à la révélation ni accompli la prière, mais il a démenti le Coran et s'en est détourné, puis il s'en est allé vers les siens en marchant avec arrogance. Al-Tabari, citant Qatada et Ibn Zayd, explique ces termes par le démenti du Livre de Dieu et la désobéissance à Dieu. Al-Mawardi et al-Zamakhshari retiennent aussi l'idée que le verbe « sadaqa » peut signifier attester le Prophète ou s'acquitter de l'aumône ; la plupart préfèrent le premier sens. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi notent que « la » est ici une négation équivalente à « lam », selon al-Kisa'i et al-Akhfash.

Au sujet du verbe « yatamatta » (marcher avec fierté), Zayd ibn Aslam le rattache à la démarche du clan de Banu Makhzum, tandis qu'al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari le rattachent à l'idée d'étirer le corps, et d'autres à « al-mata », le dos. Quant à la formule « awla laka fa-awla », elle est pour al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir une menace répétée et une imprécation, pour Ibn Juzayy une menace, et selon Ibn 'Atiyya elle a le sens de « bien plus digne de ce châtiment ». Enfin, la question « L'homme croit-il qu'il sera laissé sans rien ? » est interprétée par Ibn Zayd et Mujahid comme absence d'obligation ou d'ordre, et par al-Suddi comme absence de résurrection ; Ibn Kathir estime que le sens englobe les deux cas.

Ce passage décrit l'homme qui n'a ni cru ni prié, mais qui a démenti et s'est détourné, puis s'en est allé vers les siens en se pavanant. La plupart des commentateurs affirment que ces versets ont été révélés au sujet d'Abu Jahl, comme le rapportent Ibn Abbas, Qatada et Ibn Zayd, tandis qu'al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari les rattachent à l'homme mentionné au début de la sourate, ce qui leur donne une portée générale. Le sens de « ne pas croire » fait débat : selon Ibn Abbas, al-Qurtubi et al-Nasafi, il s'agit de la foi en la mission prophétique et au Coran, tandis que d'autres y voient le fait de ne pas donner l'aumône, et Ibn Juzayy et Ibn Ashur retiennent le premier sens. Le mot yatamma signifie se pavaner, selon la majorité, ou bien tordre le dos (mataa), ou encore s'étirer avec orgueil, selon d'autres explications. La formule « awla laka fa-awla » est une menace répétée ; Ibn Abbas et Qatada y voient l'équivalent de « que le mal t'échoie », al-Asmai la lit comme une proximité de la perdition, et Ibn Jinni et d'autres la considèrent comme un mot à sens de malheur. Le passage se termine par un rappel de la création de l'homme à partir d'une goutte de liquide, puis d'une adhérence, puis de sa formation harmonieuse, ce que les commentateurs utilisent pour affirmer la capacité de Dieu à ressusciter les morts ; certains rapportent que le Prophète disait alors « Gloire à Toi, et oui ».

Ce passage décrit l'homme obstiné qui n'a ni cru au Coran ni prié, mais a démenti et s'est détourné, puis s'en est allé vers les siens en se pavanant, plein de suffisance. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens de « yatamatta » : marcher avec affectation et orgueil. Ils divergent sur l'étymologie du mot. Selon al-Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Juzayy et d'autres, il vient de « al-mata », le dos, car le fier-à-bras tord son dos en marchant. Selon Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Sa'di, il vient de « tamattut », l'étirement, car celui qui se pavane allonge ses pas. Al-Samani rappelle que le même verbe peut aussi désigner l'étirement de la paresse ou de la maladie.

La plupart des exégètes, dont al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi, rapportent que ces versets visent Abu Jahl, et précisent que cette démarche était celle des Banu Makhzum, son clan, dont il avait l'habitude. Ils citent aussi l'épisode où le Prophète saisit Abu Jahl dans la vallée de La Mecque et lui dit « awla laka fa-awla », ce qui fut interprété comme une menace répétée. Ibn Kathir rapporte que ces mots furent prononcés par le Prophète lui-même avant d'être révélés. Le sens courant de « awla laka » est un souhait de malheur ou une menace, et plusieurs commentateurs, dont al-Qurtubi, y voient une formule de proximité du châtiment.

À propos de « yuhsaba sudan », Ibn Zayd et al-Sudi entendent « négligé, sans ordre ni interdit », tandis que Mujahid y voit l'absence de châtiment, et Ibn Kathir considère que le verset vise à la fois ce monde et la résurrection.

Ce verset, tiré de la sourate al-Qiyama, blâme l'homme impie et obstiné qui n'a ni cru à la révélation ni prié, qui a démenti et s'est détourné, puis s'en est allé vers sa famille en se pavanant par orgueil. Les commentateurs, dans leur grande majorité, disent qu'il s'agit d'Abu Jahl, et l'appuient sur sa démarche connue chez le clan de Makhzum. Quant à l'expression « awlâ laka fa-awlâ », ils divergent sur son sens. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Kalbi et Muqatil y voient une menace signifiant « malheur à toi », et disent que le Prophète ﷺ la prononça envers Abu Jahl en le saisissant, avant que le Coran ne la reprenne. Qatada la lit comme une menace sur une menace, et Ibn Kathir et Ibn Atiyya y voient une formule de malédiction souhaitant que le malheur atteigne la personne visée. Al-Asma'i la comprend comme signifiant que la perdition est proche, avis qu'apprécie Tha'lab, tandis que d'autres penchent pour « tu en es plus digne ». Sur « Croit-il que l'homme sera laissé sans but (sudan) », Ibn Zayd et al-Suddi y lisent qu'il ne sera pas ressuscité, alors que Mujahid et al-Shafi'i y lisent qu'il ne sera ni commandé ni interdit. Dieu rappelle ensuite la création de l'homme à partir d'une goutte de sperme pour prouver sa capacité à ressusciter les morts, et il est rapporté que le Prophète ﷺ disait « bala » lors de la récitation de ce passage, d'où la recommandation de le dire.

Les commentateurs expliquent que la formule « Aulā laka fa-aulā, thumma aulā laka fa-aulā » est une menace répétée pour insister. Le sens commun est que le malheur ou la chose détestable est plus proche et plus digne de celui à qui elle s'adresse. Selon la majorité, le verset vise Abu Jahl, qui marchait avec suffisance, une démarche connue chez les Banu Makhzum. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent que le Prophète ﷺ l'a saisi et lui a adressé ces paroles, à quoi Abu Jahl a répondu par un défi, avant d'être tué à Badr. Quant au mot aulā, al-Asmaʿi le rattache à la proximité de la perdition, tandis que d'autres y voient le sens de malédiction, ou une formule signifiant « tu le mérites davantage ». Abu Hayyan et al-Qurtubi notent que la répétition peut correspondre à différents moments : la vie, la mort, la résurrection et l'entrée en Enfer. Al-Wahidi et la majorité voient dans la répétition une simple insistance. Ibn Ashur juge que le verset peut viser tout incroyant, et qu'Abu Jahl en est le premier exemple. Les commentateurs divergent sur la vérité de l'occasion de révélation, al-Razi et al-Qasimi ne tranchant pas nettement.

Dieu interroge ici sur un ton de réprobation : l'homme croit-il qu'il sera laissé sans rien, livré à lui-même ? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et la plupart des commentateurs anciens expliquent « sudan » par « en vain », sans commandement ni interdit, à la manière d'une bête qui paît sans berger. Ibn Kathir précise que le verset englobe les deux états : l'homme n'est pas abandonné dans cette vie sans ordre ni défense, ni laissé dans sa tombe sans résurrection. Le Sayyid Qutb et Ibn 'Ashur y voient une invitation à reconnaître un sens et une finalité à la vie. Pour as-Suddi, le sens est qu'il ne sera pas ressuscité ; pour Ibn Zayd, qu'aucune œuvre ne lui est imposée ; pour ash-Shafi'i et d'autres, qu'il ne sera ni récompensé ni châtié. Ibn al-Qayyim fait remarquer que ces avis se rejoignent, car récompense et châtiment découlent du commandement et de l'interdiction. Al-Razi en tire un argument rationnel en faveur de la résurrection : la sagesse divine exige la responsabilité puis la rétribution. Le verset s'appuie ensuite sur la création de l'homme, d'une goutte de liquide séminal jusqu'à l'être achevé, homme ou femme, pour conclure que celui qui a créé peut ressusciter. Le Prophète, selon les récits rapportés, disait à la fin de la sourate « Subhanaka wa bala ». Quelques lecteurs ont lu « yumna » au féminin ou au masculin, selon qu'ils rapportent le mot à la goutte ou au liquide.

Ce verset rappelle à celui qui nie la résurrection son origine : n'était-il pas une goutte de liquide séminal éjaculée dans le ventre, puis une adhérence de sang, que Dieu a façonnée et harmonisée ? Les commentateurs en tirent la même conclusion : celui qui a créé l'homme ainsi ne peut être empêché de le ressusciter, et Dieu ne laisse pas l'homme sans ordre, sans commandement ni rétribution. Les lectures diffèrent sur le mot « yumna » : la majorité lit « tumna » (au féminin, se rapportant à la goutte), tandis que Hafs, Ibn Amir et Ya'qub lisent « yumna » (au masculin, se rapportant au liquide). Al-Tabari estime que les deux lectures sont correctes et de sens juste. La plupart expliquent « tumna » par « répandue » ou « versée » dans l'utérus, mais Ibn 'Ashur remarque que ce sens n'est pas attesté clairement dans les dictionnaires et juge plus probable le sens d'« émettre ». Pour « fa-khalaqa fa-sawwa », al-Mawordi et al-Razi proposent deux sens : la détermination et l'ajustement, ou le fait d'insuffler l'esprit, avis attribué à Ibn 'Abbas et Muqatil. Ibn Juzayy et Ibn 'Ashur voient dans « 'alaqa » un sang coagulé. Plusieurs commentateurs rapportent que le Prophète ﷺ, en récitant « Ne Lui est-Il pas capable de ressusciter les morts ? », disait « Gloire à Toi, et oui ». Ibn Kathir note que les chaînes de transmission de ces récits varient et que certaines sont faibles.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset s'inscrit dans l'argumentation en faveur de la résurrection par la création première de l'homme. Dieu rappelle que l'être humain n'était qu'une goutte de sperme versée dans l'utérus, puis il devint un caillot de sang, puis Dieu le façonna et harmonisa ses membres, avant de créer de lui les deux sexes, le mâle et la femelle. Ibn Abbas et d'autres entendent le mot « fakhalaqa » comme l'insufflation de l'esprit, tandis qu'al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari le comprennent comme le fait de déterminer et d'équilibrer la forme. Les lecteurs ont divergé sur « tumnā » (au féminin, se rapportant à la goutte) ou « yumnā » (au masculin, se rapportant au sperme), et al-Tabari juge les deux lectures correctes. Tous concluent que celui qui a créé l'homme ainsi est capable de le ressusciter, ce qui constitue une interpellation et une preuve contre les négateurs. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari et d'autres rapportent que le Prophète, en récitant ce passage, disait « Gloire à Toi, et oui », tradition transmise par Abu Dawud et d'autres. Plusieurs commentateurs rattachent la sourate à Abu Jahl, tandis qu'Ibn Juzayy et d'autres estiment que le sens est général.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset fait partie de l'argumentation en faveur de la résurrection : Celui qui a créé l'homme d'une goutte d'eau méprisable, puis d'une adhérence de sang, puis l'a façonné harmonieusement et en a tiré les deux sexes, le mâle et la femelle, est capable de ressusciter les morts. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi comprennent que Dieu a fait naître de cet homme des enfants, mâles et femelles, tandis que al-Nasafi et Abu al-Su'ud rapportent « de lui » au liquide séminal, c'est-à-dire que les deux sexes sont issus de la semence ; al-Razi, lui, parle des deux espèces humaines. Les exégètes s'accordent sur le sens de réprimande envers celui qui croit qu'il sera laissé sans but. Plusieurs, dont al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Kathir, rapportent que le Prophète, paix et bénédiction sur lui, disait « Gloire à Toi, et oui » en récitant ce passage ; Ibn Juzayy le mentionne également. Ibn 'Ashur et al-Qurtubi notent que l'expression désigne le plus souvent les deux sexes, sans traiter davantage la question. Sur la lecture de « yumna », la majorité lit avec la taa, tandis que Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin et Ya'qub lisent avec la ya ; al-Tabari juge les deux lectures correctes. Pour « yumna », certains l'entendent au sens d'être répandu ou versé dans l'utérus, d'autres au sens de créer. Le Razi et al-Tabari soulignent la progression des étapes de la création comme preuve de la puissance divine.

Ce passage de la sourate al-Qiyama affirme que Celui qui a créé l'homme d'une goutte de sperme éjaculée, puis d'un caillot de sang, qu'il l'a façonné et lui a donné la forme d'un homme ou d'une femme, est bien capable de ressusciter les morts. Les commentateurs expliquent que la question est une mise en garde et une réponse à ceux qui jugent la résurrection impossible : celui qui a commencé la création peut la recommencer. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi comprennent surtout le verset comme un argument tiré de la première création. Al-Razi et Ibn al-Qayyim y voient aussi une preuve par la sagesse : celui qui a perfectionné l'homme à travers ses étapes ne le laisserait pas sans ordre, sans reddition de comptes et sans rétribution. Les lecteurs divergent sur le mot « yumna » : la lecture avec le ta' le rapporte à la goutte, celle avec le ya' au sperme ; al-Tabari juge les deux lectures correctes et de même sens. Plusieurs récits rapportent que le Prophète, lorsqu'il récitait ce verset, disait « Gloire à Toi, et oui ». Ibn Kathir note que ces transmissions ont des chaînes de valeur inégale. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que le verset vise à confondre les négateurs de la résurrection, que la question suppose une réponse affirmative, et que la réponse attendue est « Bien sûr que oui ».
en: God swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul that people will be raised and judged, and then rebukes the disbeliever who thinks God will not gather his bones after they have been scattered. Commentators differ on the particle lā at the start: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Ubayda take it as merely emphatic, meaning 'I swear'; al-Farra sees it as a rejection of the deniers of resurrection before the oath begins; Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash reads it as strengthening the oath, like 'no, by God'. All agree that the Day of Resurrection is the object sworn by. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the view that God also swears by the self-reproaching soul, while al-Hasan reports that He swore only by the Day. On the self-reproaching soul, al-Hasan says it is the believer's soul, which always blames itself; Ibn Abbas and Qatada say it is the wicked soul; Mujahid says it regrets what has passed and blames itself for both wrongdoing and failing to do more good. The man referred to is understood as the disbeliever who denies resurrection, and God is able not only to gather the bones but to restore the fingertips perfectly. Al-Zamakhshari and others note the fineness of the extremities. Most exegetes explain that God could make the fingers into a single hoof-like mass so the hand could not be used, while others take it as the perfect restoration of the fingers. The passage goes on to say that man wants to continue in sin, mockingly asks when the Day will come, and will be told on that Day of all he has done.

God swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul. Most commentators, such as al-Tabari, al-Farra' and al-Baghawi, understand that God swears by both, and that the initial "la" is either an emphasis or a rebuttal of those who deny resurrection. In the reading attributed to al-Hasan and al-A'raj, "la-uqsimu" with the joined lam, the oath concerns only the Day of Resurrection, and al-Hasan holds that God did not swear by the self-reproaching soul. The meaning of "al-nafs al-lawwama" is disputed: al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrima say it is the soul that blames its owner for both good and evil, Mujahid says it is the soul that regrets what has passed, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada say it is the blameworthy or wicked soul, and al-Farra' holds that every soul, righteous or wicked, blames itself. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the view that it blames its owner for both good and evil and regrets what has passed, while al-Hasan observes that the believer is always seen reproaching himself, whereas the wicked man goes on without taking account. The following verse gives the answer of the oath, which is resurrection: man thinks God will not gather his bones, and God replies that He is able not only to gather them but to restore his fingertips perfectly, according to most exegetes, or, in the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others, that He could make his hand like a camel's hoof.

This verse affirms, through God's oath by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul, that the resurrection will certainly take place. It then rebukes the disbelieving human who thinks God will not gather his bones after they have scattered and decayed. The answer is that God is able to do so, and even able to do something greater: to restore with precision the very tips of his fingers as they were. Commentators identify this person as the disbeliever who denies the resurrection, and some reports name him as Adi ibn Rabi'a or Abu Jahl, though the meaning extends to every denier. On the particle "la" in "la uqsimu", al-Tabari cites Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu Ubayda who consider it superfluous, so the sense is simply "I swear", while al-Farra' sees it as a rejection of the deniers' claims, and others see it as mere emphasis. As for "the self-reproaching soul", al-Hasan takes it to be the soul of the believer, which never stops blaming itself, while Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean the sinful or blameworthy soul, and Mujahid the soul that regrets what has passed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the view that God swears by both. On "bala qadirin", al-Farra' treats the word as a state of the verb, meaning that we are able, while most exegetes understand that God could make the fingers like a camel's hoof, rendering them useless, and al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba read it as the ability to gather tiny bones, which makes gathering large ones easier. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, find the first reading closer to the context of the verse.

This verse answers those who doubt that the bones can be gathered after death. Most commentators explain that God affirms His ability to do so, and even to do something more delicate: to restore the fingertips exactly as they were. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya read it as meaning that God will gather them while being able to do far more. According to Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, Ikrima and al-Dahhak, God could also make a person's fingers into one smooth piece like a camel's hoof or a donkey's hoof, which would prevent fine work such as writing or sewing; this is the view of most exegetes. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba understand it instead as restoring the tiny finger bones, since whoever can gather the small can surely gather the large. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya favour the first reading, which fits the context of denial, while al-Razi also judges it closer to the truth. The word banan means the fingers or their tips, and its mention stands for the whole body, since it is the last part to be completed in creation. Some read qadirun in the nominative, while others take qadirin as a state of the implied verb. A report about Adi ibn Rabi'a is cited, which al-Baghawi notes lacks a chain of transmission, yet all the views share the same core: an affirmation of God's power to resurrect.

The commentators explain that a person does not fail to recognize God's power to gather his bones after death, but he wants to keep going forward in his sins and persist in wickedness for the rest of his life, always postponing repentance. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain that he advances his sin and delays repentance, saying "I will repent later." Al-Dahhak understood it as hope that occupies a person and keeps him from remembering death. Ibn Abbas in another report, and Ibn Zayd, took fujur to mean denying what lies ahead, namely the resurrection and the reckoning, citing the next words, "He asks when the Day of Resurrection will be," meaning mockingly and in disbelief. Ibn al-Qayyim holds this view to be stronger, because the particle "bal" and the whole context censure the one who denies the Last Day, not merely the sinner.

Al-Tabari notes that the root of fujur means to deviate from the truth, which is why the disbeliever and the wrongdoer are both called fajir. The general sense on which the commentators agree is that of a stubborn person set on error, pursuing his desires. Al-Hasan reports that the believer keeps blaming himself, while the wicked one goes on without calling himself to account.

The commentators differ on the pronoun in "amamahu": it may refer to the person, meaning the remainder of his life, or to the Day of Resurrection, which he wishes to see only after multiplying his sins. Al-Zamakhshari takes the lam in "liyafjura" to express purpose.

The disbeliever who denies the Resurrection asks when the Day of Judgment will come, mocking and doubting it. The commentators explain that ayyan means "when," and that the question expresses denial, derision or astonishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect the verse with the preceding one: the person wants to persist in his sins and postpones repentance, so he mocks the announcement of the Hour. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur read the question as mockery or as surprise at a resurrection they consider impossible. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see in it a refusal of the afterlife rooted in the desire for pleasures. Ibn al-Qayyim understands it as an outright denial of the Last Day rather than mere disobedience. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari note that the answer follows at once: the Hour will come when the eyes are dazzled, the moon is eclipsed and the sun and moon are joined. The commentators agree on the general meaning of the verse, and their differences concern mainly the meaning of fujur, of sin, and of the question itself.

This verse describes the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. According to the commentators, the eye is dazzled and bewildered, fixed in fright and unable to blink, the moon loses its light, and the sun and moon are joined in the loss of their radiance. Man then cries out: where is the escape? The commentators generally see these as signs of the end of the world, and the human being searches in vain for refuge. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read the word as baraqa with a fatha, meaning to be opened wide or to stare fixedly, while most readers use bariqa with a kasra, meaning to be terrified and stunned. Al-Tabari prefers the kasra reading and cites Arabic poetry in support, while noting that some link the fatha reading to the moment of death. Al-Hasan places it on the Day of Resurrection. As for the refuge, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr explain that there will be no fortress, no mountain and no place of safety, and that the word wizr means any shelter one takes refuge in. Ibn Kathir adds that the eyes are overwhelmed by the greatness of these events. Ibn Ashur observes that the passage is a warning presented as if it specified the time of the Hour. The disagreement thus concerns chiefly when the dazzling of the eye occurs, at the moment of death for some and on the Day itself for others, though most treat these as signs of the Resurrection.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the terror of the Day of Resurrection: the eye is dazzled and stares in fear, the moon loses its light, and then the sun and moon are brought together and their light vanishes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take khasafa al-qamar to mean that the moon's light is gone or dimmed; some readers use the passive form. Abu Hatim distinguishes kusuf (partial loss of light) from khusuf (total loss), while others treat the two as synonyms. As to when this happens, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari place it on the Day of Resurrection, whereas al-Razi allows that the dazzled gaze may refer to the moment of death. On the verb baraqa, most readers use the kasra, meaning to be bewildered and stunned, while Nafi' and Aban read the fatha, meaning to gleam or stare fixedly; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy report both without choosing between them. When the human asks where he can flee, he is told there is no refuge or stronghold, and that the final resting place is with his Lord. The commentators agree that a person will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind, but differ on the meaning: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud say his deeds and the practice he left after him; Mujahid says his first and last deeds; Zayd ibn Aslam says his wealth given in life or left to heirs.

This verse describes the terrors of the Day of Resurrection: the eye is dazed and stares in terror, the moon loses its light, and the sun and moon are brought together. The commentators differ on the meaning of this joining. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, as reported by al-Baghawi, say that they rise from the west black and folded like two bulls, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan generally agree that they are joined in the loss of their light. Al-Razi lists several explanations, including that they meet, or that they are gathered together in the extinguishing of their light. 'Ata' ibn Yasar reports that they will be cast into the sea and become the great fire of God. As for the word 'barraqa', al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain it as bewilderment and confusion, whereas Mujahid links it to death. The verse then has the human being ask where he can flee, and the following verses make clear that there is no refuge that day.

This verse describes the disbelieving person on the Day of Resurrection, when its terrors unfold: seized with dread, he cries out, where is the escape? The commentators differ on when these signs occur. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi place them on the Day of Resurrection, while Mujahid holds that the staring eye refers to the moment of death. All agree on the meaning: there is no flight and no refuge, and God's answer, no, there is no shelter, means that no fortress or mountain protects, and that the return is to the Lord alone. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that the word insan here usually means the disbeliever. The reading of barqa with a fatha, reported from Nafi, and with a kasra, followed by most, are judged by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to be close in meaning: the gaze that becomes fixed or the dazed bewilderment. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain the eclipse as the loss of light, and the joining of the sun and moon as either their being rolled up together or cast into the sea or fire, according to views transmitted from Ata ibn Yasar. Regarding al-Mafarr, the open vowel reading is a verbal noun, while the reading with a kasra denotes the place of flight, as al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud reported. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Ashur see the question as an expression of terror or despair.

The commentators explain that the words "Kallā, lā wazar" are a rebuke to the person who seeks to flee on the Day of Judgment, and that "wazar" means a refuge or stronghold to which one resorts. Originally it meant a high mountain to which the Arabs fled in fear; al-Hasan, Mutarrif and al-Dahhak therefore read it as "no mountain", while Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ikrima render it as "no fortress, no escape, no refuge". All agree that on that day a man will find no place to flee to. The final resting place is with the Lord: Ibn Zayd takes it to mean that the people of Paradise settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, Ibn Mas'ud reads it as the return and the final destination, and al-Sudi and Qatada as the ultimate end. As for the word "mafarr", most read it with a fatha on the fa' as the noun of flight, while Ibn Abbas understood it as the place of flight. The word "al-insan" in this passage generally refers to the unbeliever who denies resurrection. Several add that on that day man will be told what he did of good or evil and what he left behind, including any lasting practice, good or bad, that was followed after him, and that his own limbs will testify against him even if he offers excuses.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection a person will find no refuge or escape, and that the final return and resting place belongs to God alone. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Muqatil explain "li-yafjura amamahu" as persisting in sins and delaying repentance, while al-Dahhak sees it as hope that makes one forget death, and Ibn Zayd, with one report from Ibn 'Abbas, takes it as denial of what lies ahead, namely resurrection and reckoning. As for "al-mustaqarr", commentators give two readings: the final end and return, held by Qatada, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi, or the abode of the blessed in Paradise and of the damned in Hell, held by Ibn Zayd. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and al-Tha'alibi add that this final abode is left to God's will. On "la wazar", most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid, take it to mean no mountain, fortress or shelter, since a wazar is any place one takes refuge in. Regarding "bariqa al-basar", the majority reading with a kasra means being dazed and bewildered, whereas Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha, meaning the gaze becomes fixed; according to Mujahid this happens at death. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the person will be a witness against himself, as his own limbs testify even if he offers excuses.

This verse says that on that Day a person will be told what he sent forward and what he left behind. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud explain that the first means his deeds before death, and the second means good or bad traditions he started that others followed after him. Mujahid and al-Nakha'i take it as the beginning and end of his actions, while Ikrima takes it as the evil he did and the good he neglected. Ibn Abbas in another report and Qatada contrast the disobedience he committed with the obedience he abandoned, and Qatada adds that the neglected part concerns God's rights he failed to keep. Zayd ibn Aslam relates it to wealth he spent during his life and what he left to his heirs. Al-Tabari prefers a general reading that includes all of these meanings without singling one out. On the phrase that man is a witness against himself, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil say his own limbs bear witness, while others understand that he himself is the witness; al-Akhfash reads the feminine ending as intensification. Most commentators take the phrase even if he offers his excuses to mean even if he argues his case, while Dahhak and al-Suddi read the word as curtains. Several scholars note that the verse especially concerns the unbeliever.

The commentators explain that on the Day of Resurrection a person will be a clear proof and a witness against himself, so that no one needs to report his deeds to him, since his own limbs will speak of what he did. Most agree that the word basira means a witness or a manifest proof, and that the witnesses against him are his own limbs: his hearing, sight, hands and feet, as Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Muqatil and al-Kalbi state. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari support this reading with the verse: 'Read your record; sufficient is yourself as a reckoner against you this Day.' Some, such as al-Akhfash and al-Farra', take basira as a discerning eye or a reason that distinguishes good from evil. Others, such as al-Hasan and Qatada, understand it as a person keen to see the faults of others yet blind to his own. As for 'even if he presents his excuses', most explain that excuses will not be accepted, because a witness from within himself will contradict them. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi take 'ma'adhir' to mean curtains that conceal deeds, so that the self still bears witness even behind them. Al-Tabari prefers the reading of vain excuses. The feminine form of basira is explained either as intensive or as referring to the limbs.

This verse says that on the Day of Judgment a person will be a witness against himself, and even if he offers every excuse, those excuses will not benefit him. The commentators agree on the general sense but explain the word "ma'adhir" (excuses) in two closely related ways. The majority, including Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya, understand it as the excuses and arguments by which a person tries to clear himself, which will not be accepted because his own body testifies against him; some add that he argues falsely and his own testimony refutes him. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Muqatil and al-Kalbi take "basira" to mean the limbs themselves: hearing, sight, hands and feet. Abu al-'Aliya and 'Ata' take it as a witness against oneself. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash say the feminine ending in "basira" is for emphasis, as in "fulan hujja", while others treat it as an adjective of an eye or a proof. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi read "ma'adhir" as curtains: even if a man draws his curtains to hide his deeds, his own soul bears witness against him, a view also given by al-Zajjaj. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading as closer to the wording of the text, noting that the testimony of the self is stronger than a false excuse.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ not to move his tongue with the Quran when it is revealed, in haste to memorise it, and assures him that its gathering in his heart and its recitation are guaranteed by God. Commentators agree that God guarantees the memorisation and the recitation, that the Prophet should listen to Gabriel and then recite as he was taught, and that God will explain its meanings and rulings. Ibn Abbas, reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim, says the Prophet moved his lips for fear of forgetting, which is why the verse was sent down. Al-Sha'bi attributes it to his love for the revelation and the sweetness he found in it, while Ibn Zayd understands that he should not speak of the revelation until it is completed. On the word 'qur'anahu', Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it as recitation or memorisation, while others read it as the gathering and composing of the verses. The meaning of 'bayanahu' also varies: Qatada takes it as explaining what is lawful and unlawful, Ibn Abbas as the Prophet reciting it as Gabriel taught him, and al-Hasan as the reckoning on the Day of Judgement. Al-Razi links the verse to what precedes it, since haste is blameworthy even in religious matters. On the radiant faces looking at their Lord, Ibn Kathir and most scholars affirm that believers will see God, whereas Mujahid explains the looking as expecting reward, a view Ibn Kathir rejects.

These verses state that God took upon Himself, for His Prophet ﷺ, the gathering of the Qur'an in his heart, the ease of reciting it, and the explanation of its meanings and rulings. The commentators explain the prohibition on moving the tongue in two main ways. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, followed by Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, report that the Prophet ﷺ moved his lips and tongue when revelation came down, fearing he would forget it, so he was commanded to listen silently until Gabriel finished, and only then to recite. Others, such as al-Hasan and Qatada in one report, say he kept reciting it out of fear of forgetting, and God reassured him that He would make him retain it.

Most exegetes agree that the gathering means keeping it in his heart and that the 'recitation' refers to his reading it. Qatada also takes the word to mean memorising and composing it, while al-Dahhak understands it as fixing it in the heart. On the phrase 'follow its recitation', Ibn 'Abbas reads it as listening attentively, whereas Qatada and others read it as acting on its permitted and forbidden matters. Al-Tabari prefers the view that one should act on the commands and prohibitions that are recited.

As for the 'explanation', Qatada takes it to mean clarifying what is lawful and unlawful, Ibn 'Abbas to mean making it clear through the Prophet's tongue, and al-Hasan to mean the recompense on the Day of Judgment. The commentaries also treat the following verses, which speak of love of the fleeting world, and of radiant faces looking at their Lord. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, take this as a real vision, while the Mu'tazilite al-Zamakhshari reads the looking as hoping for reward.

This verse reports that God takes upon Himself the gathering of the Qur'an in the Prophet's heart and its recitation to him. When Gabriel recites it, he must listen and follow, and then God takes upon Himself its explanation. The commentators agree that the pronoun 'it' refers to the Qur'an and that the prohibition against moving the tongue arose from the Prophet's eagerness to retain the revelation lest he forget it. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed for this reason: he was told to listen until Gabriel finished, then recite as he had been recited to. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak explain that he feared forgetting and repeated the recitation, and was then promised that God would make him retain it. As for 'its gathering', Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean recitation, memorisation and arrangement, and al-Farra' treats 'qur'an' and 'qira'a' as verbal nouns. For 'follow its recitation', Ibn 'Abbas speaks of listening and silence, while Qatada, and Ibn 'Abbas in another report, understand it as acting on what is lawful and unlawful, commands and prohibitions; al-Tabari prefers this second sense. For 'its explanation', Qatada understands the clarification of the lawful, the unlawful and the general and specific rulings, and Ibn 'Abbas the explanation through the Prophet's tongue. Some scholars drew from this verse the permissibility of delaying explanation, but Ibn 'Ashur finds this argument weak, since 'then' marks a difference in rank rather than in time. Al-Qaffal offers a different reading in which the address is to the human being on the Day of Judgment as his book is read to him.

This verse, placed within a passage addressed to the Prophet ﷺ about receiving revelation, states that God has undertaken to gather the Quran in his heart and to make its recitation easy, so he should not hurry ahead of Gabriel for fear of forgetting it. As for the words "then, upon Us is its explanation," the commentators offer several closely related readings. Ibn Abbas understood it as the Prophet's own explanation of the text, reciting it as he was taught. Qatada took it to mean explaining what is lawful and unlawful in it, its rulings, its general and specific meanings. Al-Hasan saw it as God's recompense on the Day of Resurrection for its promises and threats. Al-Zajjaj understood it as the sending down of the Quran in clear Arabic for people. Al-Tabari regarded as most correct the view that one should act upon what is recited, following its commands and prohibitions, with the explanation concerning its rulings. Some jurists used the verse to argue that explanation may be delayed past the moment of address. Al-Razi replied that this is not necessarily implied, and Ibn Ashur judged that argument weak, since "then" indicates a difference of rank rather than of time. Several exegetes regard the passage as a parenthetical insertion within Surat al-Qiyama, whose main theme resumes with "No indeed, you love the fleeting life and neglect the Hereafter."

This verse states that those who deny the resurrection do not reject it out of ignorance, but because they love the fleeting present life and neglect the Hereafter. Al-Tabari explains that the meaning is not what they claim, namely that they will not be raised, but rather that their love of the passing pleasures of this world leads them to prefer it over the blessings of the next life, and he cites Qatada saying that most people have chosen the hasty life. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take the address to be to the unbelievers who turn away from revelation.

Other commentators connect the verse to the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that he used to hurry to recite the Qur'an along with the angel, and that the initial "No" restrains him; they then read the passage as a rebuke to humanity, whose nature inclines it to haste. Ibn Atiyya notes that the wider meaning addresses the Quraysh, and that the sense of the phrases is left to each reader's judgement.

Readers differ on the verb form: Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya observe that the second person plural with ta' addresses the audience directly, while the third person with ya' refers to humanity in general. Al-Razi explains both usages through the rhetoric of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a return to the theme of the surah, and stresses that love of the world is blamed only when the Hereafter is neglected.

This verse addresses the deniers of the resurrection, saying that they love the hasty, fleeting world and leave the Hereafter behind. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn, take the address to be to the Quraysh of Mecca. The second-person reading (tuhibbuna, tadhurun), used in Medina and Kufa, is judged by Abu 'Ubayd and others to be more direct and more forceful; the third-person reading refers to mankind in general. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn understand 'leaving' as not doing the deeds that prepare for the Hereafter. Al-Tabari reads it as preferring worldly pleasures to the reward and bliss of the next life. Al-Mawardi records both readings, one referring to reward and one to deeds. Al-Zamakhshari explains that man, created from haste, naturally loves what is quick. Ibn 'Ashur adds that loving this world is blameworthy only when it takes precedence over the Hereafter, and not when one keeps the divine law. Abu Hayyan links the verse to the preceding warning against those who turn away from God's signs. The commentators agree that the verse warns against neglecting the Hereafter for the sake of worldly life.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the faces of the believers on the Day of Resurrection as radiant, bright, joyful and blessed with delight. Most agree that "looking at their Lord" means that they gaze upon Him. Al-Hasan, Ikrima, Ibn Abbas and the majority of exegetes understand it as seeing with the eyes, and the people of the Sunna cite this verse to affirm that believers will see God in the Hereafter, relying on the hadiths found in the two Sahihs and other collections, which Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi describe as numerous and widely transmitted. A hadith from Ibn Umar about the highest of the people of Paradise who look upon the face of God morning and evening is judged weak by some hadith scholars, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report. Mujahid explains the meaning as awaiting the reward of their Lord, and al-Zamakhshari reads the looking as a figure of hope and expectation. The Mu'tazilites likewise interpret it as awaiting mercy or reward. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan reject this reading, arguing that "nazara ila" means only sight and that joy does not go with waiting. The following verse describes the faces of the disbelievers as "basira", gloomy and scowling, expecting that a calamity breaking the spine will befall them; Mujahid understands it as a great disaster, Qatada as evil, and Ibn Zayd as entry into the Fire.

The verse describes the faces of the believers on the Day of Resurrection as radiant, bright with blessing and joy, and looking toward their Lord. The commentators agree that nadra means brightness, beauty and delight. On the meaning of looking, however, they differ. Al-Tabari, following al-Hasan al-Basri and Ikrima, takes it as beholding the Creator, and Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy read it as seeing with the eyes, relying on the authentic hadiths about the vision of God. Mujahid, and reports attributed to Ibn Umar and Ikrima, understand it as waiting for the reward from the Lord; al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy reject this, arguing that looking directed by 'ila' means seeing, while waiting does not take this construction, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as a figure of hope. Some Mu'tazilite-leaning readings speak of a bounty or a reward implied. Opposite these, dark and scowling faces expect a calamity that breaks the spine, which the commentators explain as ruin, evil or entry into the Fire. Several scholars connect these verses to the rebuke of loving the fleeting world over the Hereafter.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the faces of the wretched on the Day of Resurrection as "bāsira", meaning scowling, grim, discoloured and blackened, and that they expect a calamity that will break their backs. It stands in contrast to the radiant faces mentioned just before. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, followed by others, take the word to mean scowling and sullen, al-Suddi speaks of faces whose colours have changed, and Qatada of faces that are dark.

As for "fāqira", Mujahid understands it as a great calamity, Qatada as evil, al-Suddi as destruction, Ibn Zayd as entry into the Fire, and al-Kalbi as being veiled from the sight of the Lord. Ibn al-Musayyab calls it the back-breaking blow, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Asmai link the word to the branding of a camel's nose.

The commentators agree that the faces in question are those of disbelievers or sinners, and that the verse is set against the radiant faces. On the verb "thanna", most take it to mean certainty, al-Razi sees irony in it, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari read it as expectation. Ibn 'Ashur notes that these faces form one of two opposed groups whose difference the Day of Judgement reveals.

Overall these explanations are close to one another, and there is no major disagreement among them.

The commentators explain that this verse (75:25) describes the faces of disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection as gloomy and scowling, and that their owners expect a great calamity to befall them. As for the word fa'iqa, Mujahid says it means a calamity, Qatada evil, al-Suddi destruction, Ibn Zayd entry into the Fire, and al-Kalbi being veiled from seeing the Lord. Most lexicographers, cited by Ibn Qutayba, al-Asma'i and Abu 'Ubayda, take it to mean what breaks the spine, comparing it to the branding of a camel's nose. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the verb tazunnu here means certainty or a strong expectation, whereas others keep its ordinary sense of supposing. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari link the verse to its context, since it contrasts with the radiant faces looking at their Lord, which most scholars take to mean seeing God, while Mujahid and others read it as awaiting reward, a view Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi reject. The commentators also note that the passage rebukes those who love the fleeting life and neglect the Hereafter, and that the gloomy faces depict the state of the wretched just as the radiant faces depict the state of the blessed.

This verse describes the dying person at the moment the soul departs. The opening word « kallā » is a rebuke: one should not prefer this world to the hereafter, and death is certain to come. « When it reaches the collarbones » means the soul has risen to the upper chest, the bones around the base of the throat, an expression for the approach of death and the death rattle; the pronoun refers to the soul even though it is not mentioned. On « and it is said: who can heal him? » two readings are reported. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu Qilaba, al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima take it as a request for a healer or a reciter of charms, which some read as a despairing remark. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Jawza', al-Taymi and Muqatil take it as the words of the angels: who will bear this soul up to heaven, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment? « He is sure it is parting » means the dying person is certain he is leaving this world, his family and his wealth. On « and leg is entwined with leg », opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and others see a figure for the violent joining of the end of this world with the beginning of the hereafter; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi understand the legs of the corpse wrapped in the shroud or stiffened; al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd understand the living who prepare the body and the angels who prepare the soul. Al-Tabari prefers the first sense, given the words that follow. Finally, « To your Lord, that Day, is the driving » refers to the return to God's judgement, to Paradise or the Fire according to the commentators.

This passage of Surat al-Qiyama describes the moment of death: when the soul reaches the collarbones, that is, the throat, the final stage of life has come. Commentators explain the phrase "And it is said: who can cure him?" in several ways. According to Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Abu Qilaba, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, the family seeks a physician or a healer, but none can help. Ikrima and Ibn Zayd read the question as an expression of despair, meaning that no one can save him now. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Jawza' and Sulayman al-Taymi, followed by Muqatil, understand it as the angels asking who will carry the soul up to heaven, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment.

As for "and leg is joined to leg", most take it as an image of the intensity of the ordeal: the hardship of leaving this world joined to the hardship of the Hereafter, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said. Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Hasan take it literally, as the legs wrapped in the shroud. Qatada describes the legs twisting in agony, while al-Dahhak sees men preparing the body and angels preparing the soul. Al-Tabari holds that the phrase means the hardship of death joined to the terror of the threshold of the Hereafter.

All agree on the final clause: "To your Lord that day is the driving," meaning that each person returns to the judgment of God, either to Paradise or to the Fire.

This verse describes the moment of death, when the soul reaches the collarbones and the dying person realises that this is parting from the world. The commentators agree on the general sense: it is the extreme anguish of death. They differ on several phrases. On "Who can cure him?" (man raq), Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu Qilaba and al-Dahhak take it as a call for a physician or healer for the sick man, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, Sulayman al-Taymi, Muqatil and Abu al-Jawza' attribute the question to the angels asking who will carry the soul up, the angels of mercy or those of punishment. On "the leg is entwined with the leg", Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Rabi' read it as the joining of the trials of this world and of the next, al-Sha'bi, Abu Malik and Qatada as the dying man's legs moving or stiffening, and al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab as the legs wrapped in the shroud. Al-Tabari prefers, citing the Arab idiom "war has risen upon its leg", that it means the union of the agony of death with the terror of what follows. The word "al-masaq" is understood as the return to God, some taking it as the destination and others as the final abode. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others report these views without a clear decision.

This verse describes the moment of death: when the soul reaches the collarbones, that is the throat and upper chest, the anguish grows, and those present ask whether anyone can recite a cure or bring a physician. The dying person becomes certain that he is parting from this world, his family, and his wealth. The phrase 'and leg is entwined with leg' is read by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid as the joining of the end of worldly life with the beginning of the Hereafter, a convergence of hardships, a reading al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir accept. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it as the intensity of death's agony and the terror of the passage, with people preparing the body while angels prepare the soul. Others understand it literally as the dying man's two legs: al-Sha'bi, Qatada and Abu Malik describe them wrapping together in agony, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Musayyib describe them being wrapped in the shroud, and al-Hasan reports that they became lifeless and could no longer carry him. As for 'who will recite?', some commentators attribute the words to the bystanders, while Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Jawza attribute them to the angels asking who will lift the soul upward. The verse ends with 'to your Lord, that day, is the driving,' meaning the return to God's judgment, either to Paradise or to the Fire, which commentators present as an affirmation of resurrection and recompense.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the moment of death: when the soul reaches the collarbones at the base of the throat, those present ask whether anyone can treat or heal the dying person, and he realises that he is about to be parted from this world, his family and his possessions. Most agree that the 'driving' means being brought back to God and His judgement, where people are led either to Paradise or to the Fire. On the question of who asks 'is there a healer?', Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilaba, Qatada, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd take it as a request for treatment, whereas Abu al-Jawza' and Abu al-'Aliya understand it as the angels asking who will carry the soul up to heaven, whether angels of mercy or of punishment. The phrase 'one leg is wound around the other' has several readings: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi' and Qatada take it as a figure for the trials of this world meeting those of the next, or for extreme distress, and al-Tabari considers this the most sound view. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab take it literally, as the legs being wrapped in the shroud, while al-Dahhak says the living prepare the body while the angels prepare the soul. Regarding 'he thought it was parting', most explain that he was certain of it, since the event had not yet occurred.

The verse describes the stubborn disbeliever, whom most commentators identify as Abu Jahl: he neither believed in the message nor prayed, but instead denied the Qur'an and turned away, then went back to his people strutting in pride. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada and Ibn Zayd, explains this as denying the Book of God and turning away from obedience to Him. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari also note that the word for believing may mean affirming the Messenger or giving charity, though most prefer the first meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the particle here carries the sense of "lam" (not), following al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash.

On the word "yatamatta" (strutting), Zayd ibn Aslam links it to the gait of the Banu Makhzum, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean stretching out, and others to "al-mata", the back. The phrase "awla laka fa-awla" is read by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as a repeated threat and curse, by Ibn Juzayy as a warning, and by Ibn 'Atiyya as meaning that the person is more deserving of this punishment. Finally, the question "Does man think he will be left aimless?" is explained by Ibn Zayd and Mujahid as meaning unordered and unforbidden, and by al-Suddi as meaning not resurrected; Ibn Kathir holds that the verse covers both situations.

This passage describes a man who neither believed in the message nor prayed, but denied it, turned away, and then went back to his family strutting with pride. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, say these verses were revealed about Abu Jahl, citing Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Ashur also notes that the verses describe every disbelieving person. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi link the pronoun to the man mentioned at the start of the surah, so the meaning is general. Scholars differ on what 'did not believe' means: Ibn Abbas and al-Nasafi take it as not believing in the prophetic message, while others read it as not giving charity, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur prefer the first sense. Yatamma is explained by most as strutting, by al-Farra and al-Zamakhshari as twisting the back, and by Ibn Qutayba as stretching the limbs. The repeated threat 'awla laka fa-awla' is glossed by Ibn Abbas and Qatada as 'may evil be upon you', while al-Asmai reads it as near destruction. The passage ends by recalling the creation of man from a drop, then a clot, then his formation, which the commentators use to argue that God can raise the dead; some report that the Prophet would say 'Glory be to You, yes'.

This passage describes the stubborn person who neither believed in the Qur'an nor prayed, but denied it and turned away, then walked back to his family swaggering with pride. The commentators agree that "yatamatta" means to strut and walk with conceit. They differ on its root. Al-Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Juzayy and others derive it from "al-mata", the back, since the strutting man twists his back. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di derive it from "tamattut", stretching, because the one who struts lengthens his stride. Al-Samani notes that the word can also mean stretching out from laziness or illness.

Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that these verses concern Abu Jahl, and they note that this walk was typical of his clan, Banu Makhzum. They also cite the incident in the valley of Mecca where the Prophet seized Abu Jahl and said "awla laka fa-awla", which was taken as a repeated threat. Ibn Kathir reports that the Prophet himself spoke these words before the revelation. The usual sense of "awla laka" is a wish for misfortune or a warning, and al-Qurtubi and others take it as a sign that the punishment is near. Some, such as Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi, also give other readings, and the repetition is seen as emphasis.

On "yuhsaba an yutraka sudan", Ibn Zayd and al-Sudi understand it as left aimless, without command or prohibition, while Mujahid takes it as going unpunished. Ibn Kathir holds that the verse covers both this life and the resurrection.

This verse, from Surat al-Qiyama, condemns the stubborn disbeliever who neither affirmed the message nor prayed, who denied and turned away, and then walked back to his family with a proud swagger. Most commentators say it was revealed about Abu Jahl, citing his well-known strut, which they associate with the Banu Makhzum. The phrase 'awla laka fa-awla' is explained in several ways. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it as a threat meaning 'woe to you', and report that the Prophet grabbed Abu Jahl and said it before the Quran was revealed with the same words. Qatada reads it as a warning upon a warning, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya take it as a curse wishing harm to fall upon the addressee. Al-Asma'i understands it as meaning that ruin is near, a view Tha'lab praised, and others take it to mean that the addressee is more deserving of this punishment. On 'Does man think he will be left without purpose (sudan)', Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi read it as meaning he will not be resurrected, while Mujahid and al-Shafi'i read it as meaning he will not be commanded or forbidden. God then points to the creation of man from a drop of semen as proof of His power to resurrect, and it is reported that the Prophet would say 'bala' when reciting the verse about God's power to give life to the dead, which is why the practice is recommended.

The commentators explain that the phrase « Awla laka fa-awla, thumma awla laka fa-awla » is a threat repeated for emphasis, meaning that ruin or what is hateful is nearer to the person addressed and more fitting for him. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, say the verse concerns Abu Jahl, who walked with arrogant swagger, a gait known among the Banu Makhzum. They report that the Prophet took hold of him and spoke these words, and that Abu Jahl answered with defiance, and was later killed at Badr. On the word awla, al-Asmaʿi takes it to mean that ruin is close, others understand it as a curse, and some as meaning that the person deserves it more. Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi note that the repetition may refer to several stages: life, death, resurrection and the entry into Hell. Al-Wahidi and most others see the repetition as mere emphasis. Ibn Ashur holds that the verse may address every disbeliever, with Abu Jahl as the first example, and he considers the accounts of the occasion of revelation to be loosely reported. Commentators differ on the precise circumstances of revelation, and al-Razi and al-Qasimi do not settle the matter.

God poses here a rhetorical question of reproach: does man think he will be left aimless? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early commentators explain "sudan" as left in vain, without command or prohibition, like camels grazing without a herdsman. Ibn Kathir adds that the verse covers both states: man is not left in this world without command and prohibition, nor left in his grave without resurrection. Sayyid Qutb and Ibn 'Ashur read it as a call to recognise purpose in human life. As-Suddi takes it to mean that he will not be raised; Ibn Zayd, that no duty is imposed on him; ash-Shafi'i and others, that he will be neither rewarded nor punished. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that these views converge, since reward and punishment follow from command and prohibition. Al-Razi draws a rational argument for the resurrection from divine wisdom, which requires accountability and then recompense. The verse then argues from man's creation, from a drop of fluid to a complete human being, male or female, that the One who began creation can bring it back. According to the reports cited, the Prophet used to say "Subhanaka, wa bala" when reciting it. Some readers vary the reading of "yumna" between the feminine and masculine forms, depending on whether the word is taken to refer to the drop or to the fluid.

This verse confronts the one who denies resurrection with his own origin: was he not a drop of fluid emitted into the womb, then a clot of blood, which God shaped and formed? The commentators draw the same conclusion: the One who created man in this way cannot be incapable of raising him again, and God does not leave man without command, prohibition or recompense. The readings differ on the word yumna. Most read tumna (feminine, referring to the drop), while Hafs, Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read yumna (masculine, referring to the fluid). Al-Tabari holds that both readings are sound in meaning. Most explain the verb as meaning to be poured or spilled into the womb, though Ibn 'Ashur notes that this sense is not clearly attested in the lexicons and prefers the meaning of emitting. For fa-khalaqa fa-sawwa, al-Maturidi-style and al-Razi offer two readings: decreeing and proportioning, or breathing the spirit into him, the latter attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur take 'alaqa to be a clot of blood. Several commentators report that the Prophet, upon reciting the verse asking whether He is not able to give life to the dead, would say glory be to You, and yes. Ibn Kathir observes that the chains of transmission for these reports vary, and some are weak.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the argument for resurrection drawn from the first creation of man. God reminds the human being that he was once a drop of fluid poured into the womb, then became a clot of blood, and that God then shaped him and perfected his form, and from him made the two sexes, male and female. Ibn Abbas and others understand the word 'khalaqa' as the breathing in of the soul, whereas al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean determining the form and balancing it, and both meanings are considered possible. The readers differed over 'tumna' (feminine, referring to the drop) and 'yumna' (masculine, referring to the fluid), and al-Tabari holds that both readings are valid. All agree that the One who created man in this way is able to bring him back to life, and this is presented as a rebuke and proof against the deniers. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari transmit that the Prophet, when reciting it, would say 'Glory be to You, and yes,' a report also found in Abu Dawud. Most exegetes link the surah to Abu Jahl, though others, such as Ibn Juzayy, take the sense as general.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of the argument for resurrection: the One who created man from a humble drop of fluid, then from a clot, then formed him in perfect proportion and made from him the two sexes, male and female, is able to bring the dead back to life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand that God made from this person offspring, both males and females, while al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud refer the word 'from him' to the semen, so that both sexes come from the fluid; al-Razi speaks of the two categories of humankind. The scholars agree that the verse rebukes and denies the idea that man is left without purpose. Several, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, report that the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to say 'Glory be to You, and yes' when reciting this verse, and Ibn Juzayy also mentions it. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qurtubi observe that the expression refers mainly to the two sexes, without developing the point further. On the reading of 'yumna', the majority read it with a taa, while Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub read it with a ya; al-Tabari judges both readings valid in meaning. Some explain 'yumna' as meaning poured out into the womb, others as meaning created. Al-Razi and al-Tabari highlight the successive stages of creation as evidence of God's power.

This verse in Surat al-Qiyama affirms that the One who created man from a drop of emitted seed, then from a clinging clot, shaped him and made him male and female, is certainly able to bring the dead back to life. The commentators explain that the question is a rebuke and a reply to those who find resurrection impossible: the one who began creation can repeat it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi mostly read the verse as an argument from the first creation. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim also see a proof from wisdom: the One who perfected man through his stages would not leave him without command, prohibition and recompense. Readers differ on the word yumna: the reading with a ta' makes the drop the subject, while the reading with a ya' makes the seed the subject, and al-Tabari considers both correct and equivalent in meaning. Several reports say that the Prophet, when reciting it, would say 'Glory be to You, and yes', and Ibn Kathir notes that these transmissions have chains of differing strength. The scholars agree that the verse aims to confront those who deny resurrection, that the question implies an affirmative answer, and that the expected response is 'Yes indeed'.
